residual_disagreements.my_counterclaim: The verifier-feedback gap is real, but it is not the top-priority fix. The more fundamental flaw is that the shipped workflow is serial-turn, not symmetric: `agent_b` always writes after seeing `agent_a`'s freshest position, so a clean verifier loop on top of the current topology would still let convergence reflect second-mover accommodation rather than independent agreement.

The asymmetry is not a one-shot round-1 contamination. In every round, the graph runs `agent_a` before `agent_b`, and `agent_b` reads `latest.get(peer_name)` after `agent_a` has already updated `latest_positions`, so `agent_b` has same-round second-mover advantage throughout the run.

Ledger growth and wall-clock are real operational costs, but the first structural failure in answer quality at high round counts is debate drift from lossy memory: the debaters never see full history or verifier output, only `own_prior` plus `peer_latest`, while synthesis alone gets chronology.

I agree the verifier ledger is structurally underused and I agree it ranks #2 - but I disagree with peer's implicit framing that fixing topology first 'leaves second-mover bias intact' as if feedback is wholly downstream. Verifier feedback into _position_prompt is partially independent of topology: even in a perfectly barriered protocol, agents still cannot see lineage_flag / unverified status without the feedback edge. So #1 (barrier) and #2 (feedback) are co-required, not strictly serial; implementation order should be 'barrier then feedback' only because the barrier is a smaller graph change.

I now agree drift is the first QUALITY failure at max_rounds>5 (peer is right: debaters see only own_prior + peer_latest while synthesis alone gets chronology - deliberate.py:466-480 vs 588-589). But I still hold that the first OPERATOR-visible failure is verifier_ledger size + wall-clock: the ledger is append-only and persisted in full each round (deliberate_verifier.py:533-580), and 300s x 3 stages x N rounds dominates user-visible run time before drift becomes observable. These are different failure modes, both real; my round-1 framing conflated them.

I agree the gap is real and severity=warn is correct, but I rank it strictly BELOW evidence-semantic verification (a_evidence_locatable_not_proven). Reason: a profile hook expands what the chassis can do; evidence-semantic verification fixes whether what the chassis already produces can be trusted. Trust before reach. Peer's reviewer_summary places evidence semantics at #3 and extensibility at #4, which matches my ranking - flagging to make the agreement explicit and avoid silent reordering during synthesis.
